newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine T-bill volumes seen low after new tax.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine T-bill volumes seen low after new tax.

text.p: A 30 percent tax on Ukrainian Treasury bills that went into effect on July 1 was expected to keep T-bill volumes low at sales this week, traders said on Monday.
"There won't be great volumes due to the taxes," said Valentyn Banin, a trader at the Finance and Credit Bank. "Those who wanted to buy T-bills bought before that date."

He predicted yields -- unchanged at 20.20 percent for six-month paper, down to 28.14 percent from 28.18 on nine-month paper, steady at 30.36 percent for nine-month bills and holding at 32.56 percent for 18-month notes -- would remain steady.
"The Finance Ministry won't change the yields much more," he said.
Buyers from countries holding mutual taxation agreements with Ukraine were to be exempt from the tax on T-bills, whose profits until July 1 were tax-free.
Patricia Bartholomew, senior analyst at Wood and Company, predicted volumes would pick up from last week's sales but said they would not result in the kind of big buying seen at the end of June.
She forecast slowly falling rates due to the passage of the 1997 budget last month, Ukraine's confidence in talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and lower inflation.
"There will be a gradual fall in yields," she said, adding the drop could be 15 percent on six-month paper by the year-end.
Ukrainian officials have forecast annual inflation of 10 to 15 percent after June inflation fell to 0.1 percent from 0.8 percent in May. January to June inflation was 5.3 percent.
They have also said an IMF mission, in Kiev this week for talks on a three-year, $2.5-3 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF), would decide by August to award Ukraine the credit.
Bartholomew also predicted continuing stability for the hryvnia, on Monday unchanged on the Ukrainian Interbank Currency Exchange (UICE) at 1.8570.

Nigel Whittaker, director for Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's emerging markets department, said inflation figures and a central bank decision to lower the refinancing rate on July 8 boded well for the market.
"Things have gotten bullish," he said. "People are waiting to see if the EFF will replace the stand-by agreement."
The new IMF credit would succeed Ukraine's $867 million stand-by agreeement which expired in February.
Parliament passed the 1997 budget on June 27 after a nearly six-month delay.
